quote: our emotions arise from our models of reality
content: The essay anticipates this arrow and says what to do about it: "Your anger or calm shouldn't affect your best guess here... though it may take some effort to think that clearly." The criterion is normative. Johnson and Tversky's mood-contaminated risk estimates are cases where an emotion corrupted the map, and the rule classifies them as failures (Johnson & Tversky 1983). Schachter and Singer's misattribution result did not survive replication: aroused subjects did not take on the emotion the situation suggested, and they reported negative affect whatever the setting (Marshall & Zimbardo 1979; Maslach 1979). A rule that people can break is still a rule that can be applied.

quote: That which the truth nourishes should thrive.
content: The maxim is conditional by construction. "That which the truth nourishes" names the feelings that survive contact with the truth; it does not claim that every truth nourishes. The depressive-realism evidence is also weaker than the objection needs. The meta-analysis the note cites found the effect small and concentrated in studies without an objective accuracy criterion (Moore & Fresco 2012), and a large preregistered replication of the Alloy and Abramson paradigm found no depressive realism at all (Dev et al. 2022, Collabra: Psychology). Taylor and Brown's positive-illusions thesis ran into observer-rated data in which self-enhancers looked less well adjusted, not more (Colvin & Block 1994; Colvin, Block & Funder 1995, JPSP). For thirty years the "live dispute" has been moving toward the maxim.

quote: Since the days of Socrates at least, and probably long before, the way to appear cultured and sophisticated has been to never let anyone see you care strongly about anything.
content: The claim is about how to "appear cultured and sophisticated," and that ideal has a long record. Castiglione made sprezzatura, the studied appearance of effortlessness and unconcern, the defining grace of the courtier (1528). Chesterfield told his son that since he had had the full use of his reason, nobody had heard him laugh. Stoic apatheia, the Victorian stiff upper lip and modern cool all prize visible detachment in the same way. Homeric weeping and the cult of sensibility are real counterexamples, though sensibility was being mocked as vulgar within a generation. "Since the days of Socrates" overstates how uniform the ideal was. The essay's claim is that the posture keeps coming back and is prized among elites, and the history supports that.

quote: My sadness on waking is rational; there is no truth which destroys it.
content: The next essay states the criterion precisely: an emotion is "not rational" if it "rests on mistaken beliefs," and it is rational if correct beliefs evoke it. Grief for a fictional character rests on no mistaken belief, since the reader does not think the character existed, so the criterion does not condemn it. Moods with no propositional object fall outside the criterion's scope; they are not verdicts it gets wrong. The persistent spider phobia is where the criterion works best. The fear rests on an appraisal of danger that the person knows is false, so "the Way opposes your fear." The standard treatment, exposure therapy, is the practice of bringing the feeling into line with the known truth. A criterion that sorts some emotions and says nothing about others is a partial theory, and a partial theory is all the essay offered.
